hints.junior: A server hiccup drops everyone at once — if every client reconnects instantly, that flood is often what turns a hiccup into a real outage.
hints.mid: Instant reconnect works fine for one client's own drop, but fails badly for a correlated event that disconnects many clients at the same moment.
hints.staff: A recovering server needs headroom — an instant-retry client population removes exactly the headroom the recovery needs.

hints.junior: Click simulate disconnect a few times and watch the timestamps between reconnect attempts in each mode.
hints.mid: The broken mode's attempts land almost back to back; the fixed mode's intervals visibly grow with each attempt.
hints.staff: This shows one client's own backoff curve — the real population-level benefit is many jittered curves not overlapping, which one client can only gesture at.

hints.junior: Wait a little longer after each failed attempt — 1s, then 2, then 4 — instead of retrying instantly every time.
hints.mid: Jitter matters too — without it every client computes the same delay sequence and they all retry in sync anyway, just less often.
hints.staff: Full jitter (random between 0 and the exponential cap) spreads the retry distribution wider than small-jitter variants under real correlated load.

hints.junior: Always cap the max delay — uncapped backoff eventually makes a client wait absurdly long, which feels broken even though it's 'working as designed.'
hints.mid: Reset the backoff counter after a connection stays up a while, or one bad patch throttles every later, unrelated reconnect too.
hints.staff: Distinguish disconnect reasons where possible — a clean server-initiated close can skip the initial backoff step; an abnormal close should always back off.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about a WebSocket client that reconnected instantly after every disconnect, and how that turned a brief server hiccup into a full outage.
sections.mid: Immediate reconnect works fine for a single client dropping on its own — it fails badly when a server-side event disconnects many clients at once, since instant mass-reconnect is a self-inflicted traffic spike.
sections.staff: A recovering server needs headroom to actually recover — an instant-retry client population removes exactly that headroom.

sections.junior: The fix is exponential backoff with jitter — wait a bit longer after each failed attempt, and spread those attempts out randomly so clients don't all retry in the same instant.
sections.mid: Exponential backoff alone still has a problem — every client computes the same delay sequence, so they retry in sync. Jitter spreads those retries out across time instead.
sections.staff: Full jitter, a random delay uniformly chosen between 0 and the exponential cap, tends to outperform smaller-jitter variants under real correlated-failure load.

sections.junior: Simulate a few disconnects in each mode and watch how the timing between reconnect attempts differs.
sections.mid: The broken mode's attempts land almost immediately after each other — the fixed mode's intervals grow with each attempt.
sections.staff: This demo shows one client's own backoff curve — the real benefit is population-level, many clients' jittered curves not overlapping.

sections.junior: Don't reconnect instantly on every disconnect. Back off exponentially, add jitter, and cap the maximum delay.
sections.mid: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads reconnect attempts out over time instead of every client hammering the server in the same instant.
sections.staff: Cap the maximum delay, reset the backoff after a sustained connection, and treat different disconnect reasons differently rather than one uniform retry policy.
